To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) The Pesaran (2000) CCE and the AMG estimators solve the identification problem in standard pooled panel estimators by accounting for the common factors in the equation; (ii) the standard OLS estimator with first differenced data performs well in the presence of cross section dependence and (iii) the standard OOLS estimator with level data performs poorly.

(i) The AMG estimator is a useful and robust alternative to the CCE approach, particularly when the number of cross section observations is large; (ii) the performance of standard estimators in macro panels is not always as bad as it is sometimes reported; (iii) the use of first difference transformations can be a good alternative for standard estimators in the case of macro panels.
the standard pooled OLS estimator in levels with year dummies performs well in the case of nonstationary data with a common factor structure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a topic of considerable empirical interest and has the potential to make a significant contribution to the literature on panel data estimation.

the question of how the presence of nonstationarity and cross section dependence affect the performance of panel estimators in macro panel data and whether this is different to the findings in micro data applications.
the question of whether the use of novel panel estimators incorporating cross section dependence is warranted in the case of macro panels.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the performance of the standard panel estimators in the presence of cross section dependence and nonstationarity depends on the nature of the cross section dependence and the degree of nonstationarity.

the performance of standard (micro) panel estimators in nonstationary panels depends on the specific characteristics of the data generating process and is not always inferior to that of novel panel estimators.
the performance of standard estimators is sensitive to the nature of the cross section dependence and the degree of nonstationarity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the AMG estimator performs well in most of our Monte Carlo experiments.
the AMG estimator performs best in all setups, but the CCE estimator is a close second.

the AMG and Pesaran (2000) CCE approaches are the preferred estimation methods for macro panel data with cross section dependence, but the standard pooled estimators can be a reasonable alternative if the cross section dependence is weak or the variables are in first difference.
The main takeaway from our work is that
standard pooled OLS estimators are often not as bad as previously thought, especially if the data generating process involves a high degree of cross section dependence.
there are no clear winners among the various approaches considered.
the performance of standard pooled estimators in macro panels can be very different from what is observed in micro panels.
